description: Macrophages are recruited to tissues by chemotactic gradients, and this recruitment has to be damped as well as driven, or inflammatory infiltrate persists and causes collateral tissue damage. Negative regulation of macrophage chemotaxis covers the signals that slow or stop that directed migration, restraining how many macrophages arrive at a site of injury or infection and how far they move once there. The genes involved act at several levels: secreted cytokine-like mediators and their receptor engagement, a complement component whose cleavage products are themselves chemoattractants and therefore a point of gradient control, a matrix metalloproteinase implicated in limiting macrophage recruitment, a signalling adaptor, and an immune-cell surface receptor of the SLAM family. An estrogen-synthesising enzyme links steroid hormone status to the strength of the response, one route by which sex hormones shape inflammation and the resolution phase of wound healing.

Granulocyte production from myeloid progenitors must be held in check as well as driven, and this set covers the braking side: processes that slow or block commitment of progenitors to the neutrophil and eosinophil lineages. Restraint matters because unchecked granulopoiesis distorts the balance between granulocytes, monocytes and dendritic cells, and loss of these controls contributes to myeloid leukaemias and to inflammatory tissue damage. The transcriptional arm includes RUNX1 and the retinoic acid receptor RARA, whose fusion in acute promyelocytic leukaemia freezes cells at the promyelocyte stage, alongside PRDM16 and ZBTB46, the latter marking classical dendritic cells rather than granulocytes. Signalling and degradation components contribute too: the inositol phosphatase INPP5D dampens phosphoinositide-dependent growth factor responses, TRIB1 directs turnover of myeloid transcription factors, and CUL4A supplies ubiquitin ligase activity. Together they set lineage output and the pace of emergency granulopoiesis.

Mast cells release histamine, proteases and other preformed mediators within seconds of activation, so restraining that release sets the threshold for allergic and anaphylactic reactions. Negative regulation of mast cell degranulation keeps resting mast cells quiescent and limits mediator output once IgE crosslinks the high-affinity IgE receptor, protecting tissues from unnecessary bronchoconstriction, vascular leak and itch; loss of this brake underlies atopic disease and mast cell hyperreactivity. The inhibitory arm works partly through surface immunoreceptors carrying tyrosine-based inhibitory motifs, such as CD300A, which counter activating signals at the membrane, and partly through lectin-mediated engagement of mast cell surface receptors by galectin-9. Intracellularly, RABGEF1 restrains signalling downstream of receptor engagement, and its absence produces spontaneous skin inflammation in mice. The pathway sits within innate immune tolerance and the control of type I hypersensitivity rather than in mediator synthesis itself.

Cytosolic DNA sensing by cGAS and its adaptor STING triggers type I interferon and inflammatory gene expression, and this pathway describes the brakes that keep that response proportionate and self-limiting. Restraint matters because unchecked activation by the cell's own DNA drives interferonopathies, lupus-like autoimmunity and sterile inflammation, while excessive signalling during infection is itself damaging. The brakes act at every step: nucleases such as TREX1 degrade cytosolic DNA before it is sensed, cGAS itself is held in check by kinase- and acyltransferase-mediated modification and by nuclear tethering to chromatin via BANF1, the second messenger cGAMP is hydrolysed extracellularly, and adaptor turnover through autophagy factors and ubiquitin-ligase adaptors such as SPSB3 limits signalling duration. Phosphatase activity and DNA-damage-response proteins including PARP1 and PRKDC further couple genome surveillance to dampened interferon output.

Acute inflammation triggered by antigen must be actively damped, or immune complexes and mast cell activation drive tissue injury, anaphylaxis and autoantibody-driven disease; the genes here restrain that response rather than initiate it. The clearest example is the low-affinity IgG receptor FCGR2B, the only inhibitory Fc gamma receptor, which carries an inhibitory signalling motif and raises the threshold for B cell, mast cell and phagocyte activation by immune complexes; loss of its function predisposes to systemic autoimmunity. Neuropeptide Y acting through its receptors links neural output to immune tone, illustrating neuroimmune brake on local inflammatory responses, while sialophorin (SPN, CD43) shapes leukocyte adhesion and contact-dependent activation. Other members contribute cytokine receptor signalling and endoplasmic reticulum stress handling. Collectively this is the negative arm of hypersensitivity control, setting how strongly and how long an antigen-provoked inflammatory episode proceeds.

Neutrophils are the first cells recruited to infection or injury, and the braking mechanisms that damp their migration determine whether that response resolves or becomes tissue-destroying. Negative regulation of neutrophil migration covers signals that reduce the rate and extent of chemotactic movement out of the vasculature and through tissue, limiting collateral damage in conditions such as acute lung injury, ischemia-reperfusion and chronic inflammatory disease. The genes here act at several levels: SLIT2 signals through Robo receptors to repel chemotaxing neutrophils and stabilise their cytoskeleton, C5AR2 serves as a non-canonical receptor for the complement fragment C5a that tempers signalling through the classical C5a receptor, TNFAIP6 modifies hyaluronan-rich matrix to interfere with adhesion and extravasation, and the microRNA MIR223 restrains myeloid activation transcriptionally. Together they represent the resolution side of innate immune recruitment rather than its initiation.

Toll-like receptor 9 detects unmethylated CpG DNA inside endosomes and drives type I interferon and inflammatory cytokine output, particularly from plasmacytoid dendritic cells; braking that response keeps recognition of self DNA from tipping into autoimmunity. Negative regulation of TLR9 signalling gathers the mechanisms that limit how strongly and how long the receptor fires, and its loss is associated with interferon-driven disease such as lupus. The genes here act at distinct points: a plasmacytoid dendritic cell surface immunoreceptor delivers an inhibitory signal that dampens interferon production, a small GTPase controls endosomal and lysosomal trafficking of the receptor and so limits its residence in the signalling compartment, and a receptor phosphatase and a lysosomal thioesterase further restrain downstream activation. Together they set the threshold for innate sensing of DNA and enforce tolerance to host nucleic acids.

Leukocytes leave the bloodstream by adhering to endothelium and squeezing between cells, and this biology restrains that step, limiting how many cells extravasate into tissue. Damping cellular extravasation keeps inflammation proportionate: without such brakes, neutrophils and monocytes accumulate in tissue and drive collateral injury, as seen in sepsis, arthritis and atherosclerotic vessel walls. The restraint comes from several directions. Chemokines such as CXCL12, CCL21, CCL25 and CCL28 pattern where cells are held or directed, and in some contexts their signalling retains cells rather than recruiting them. Prostaglandin E2 acting through the EP4 receptor raises cyclic AMP in leukocytes and endothelium to suppress adhesion, MIR146A dampens NF-κB-driven inflammatory output, and phospholipase C beta and a cytokine receptor subunit tune the downstream signalling that converts chemotactic cues into firm arrest and diapedesis.

Thymocyte expansion must be curbed as well as driven, and this pathway covers the signals that dampen proliferation of immature T cells in the thymus. Restraining the progenitor pool sets the size and timing of successive developmental stages, allowing selection to operate on a controlled number of cells; loss of such brakes contributes to thymocyte hyperplasia and lymphoid malignancy. The genes involved span secreted morphogens and cell-intrinsic cell cycle control: bone morphogenetic protein and hedgehog ligands produced by thymic stroma act on developing thymocytes to limit their expansion, a cyclin-dependent kinase inhibitor encoded at the INK4A locus enforces cell cycle arrest, and a transmembrane regulator of Wnt responsiveness tempers proliferative signalling. Together they illustrate how niche-derived cues and intracellular checkpoints converge to balance proliferation against differentiation during T cell development.

Bone mass is maintained by holding osteoclast formation in check, and this braking arm of osteoclast development limits how many bone-resorbing multinucleated cells arise from myeloid precursors. When the restraint fails, resorption outpaces formation and bone is lost, as in osteoporosis, inflammatory erosion and other high-turnover skeletal disease; excessive restraint instead gives dense, poorly remodelled bone. The genes involved act at several levels: a claudin tight-junction protein whose loss in the stomach alters systemic signals to bone, an extracellular matrix glycoprotein that sequesters TGF-beta family ligands and so tunes precursor differentiation, an F-box ubiquitin ligase substrate receptor that targets osteoclastogenic transcription factors for degradation, an inhibitory leukocyte immunoglobulin-like receptor that dampens ITAM-driven costimulation, and lactoferrin, an iron-binding secreted protein that suppresses precursor commitment while favouring osteoblasts. Together they place skeletal remodelling under immune, endocrine and matrix control.

Myeloid progenitors must be held back from becoming monocytes if the marrow is to retain proliferating precursors and generate other lineages, and this restraint on monocyte differentiation is how that balance is kept. It matters because loss of the brake shifts output toward monocytes and macrophages, while its inappropriate persistence blocks maturation, a pattern seen in myeloid leukaemias where differentiation arrest accompanies continued proliferation. The genes involved act at several levels: cell cycle and growth regulators such as CDK6 and MYC keep progenitors cycling rather than maturing, a homeobox factor and the dendritic-cell-restricted factor ZBTB46 impose alternative transcriptional programmes, the inositol phosphatase INPP5D dampens signalling downstream of growth factor and immune receptors, and a microRNA tunes the same decision post-transcriptionally. The result is a checkpoint on lineage commitment within haematopoiesis and innate immune cell supply.

Detection of cytoplasmic viral RNA by RIG-I triggers interferon production, and this braking machinery keeps that alarm proportionate and self-limiting, preventing sustained type I interferon output and the autoinflammatory or interferonopathy-like damage that follows unchecked sensing. The regulators act at several points: a RIG-I-like helicase relative, LGP2 (DHX58), competes with and modulates recognition of duplex RNA; mitochondrial proteins such as NLRX1 and C1QBP restrain the adaptor MAVS at the outer membrane; RNF125 ubiquitinates RIG-I to drive its degradation; and the NPLOC4-UFD1 partners of the p97 segregase feed sensor and adaptor components into proteasomal turnover. Together they set the threshold and duration of antiviral innate signalling, so that interferon-stimulated gene expression resolves once infection is cleared. Loss of this negative control tips the balance toward chronic inflammation, while viruses exploit the same nodes to blunt host defence.

Antibody output has to be capped as well as switched on, and this is the braking side of that balance: processes that stop or reduce immunoglobulin production by B cells. Without such restraint, plasma cell differentiation and class switching run unchecked, contributing to hypergammaglobulinaemia, autoantibody formation and allergic IgE responses. The genes here act at several levels. Inhibitory surface receptors such as CD22 and the low-affinity IgG receptor FCGR2B raise the threshold for B cell activation and deliver negative signals from immune complexes, while complement receptor CR1 tunes complement-dependent stimulation. BCL6 holds germinal centre B cells in a proliferative, differentiation-blocked state, opposing terminal plasma cell commitment. FOXP3 marks regulatory T cells that suppress the helper signals B cells require, and NDFIP1 promotes ubiquitin-mediated limitation of lymphocyte responses. Cytokine-side components, including an IL-33 and decoy IL-13 receptor pairing, link tissue signals to restraint of type 2 antibody responses.

Granulocytes are recruited to infected or damaged tissue by chemotactic gradients, and this recruitment must be braked so that neutrophil and eosinophil influx resolves rather than destroying the tissue it is meant to protect. The processes grouped here dampen granulocyte chemotaxis, and their loss favours persistent neutrophilic inflammation of the kind seen in sepsis, arthritis and chronic lung disease. The mechanisms are varied: a decoy-like receptor for complement-derived anaphylatoxins tempers signalling through the classic C5a receptor; a cell-surface peptidase trims chemokines and neuropeptides, altering their potency; a secreted guidance cue better known from axon pathfinding repels migrating leukocytes; a hyaluronan-binding inflammatory protein modifies the matrix and limits transmigration; and a myeloid microRNA restrains the granulocyte differentiation and activation programme itself. Together they place inflammation resolution alongside chemokine signalling and directed cell migration.

B cell output has to be capped, and this is the braking side of that decision: processes that slow or block progenitors from committing to and maturing along the B lineage. Restraint matters because unchecked B cell production skews the marrow toward lymphoid output at the expense of other lineages and enlarges the pool of cells that must later be screened for self-reactivity. The genes act mostly by opposing the transcriptional and signalling inputs that drive commitment — ID2 sequesters E-protein transcription factors such as E2A that would otherwise turn on the B cell programme, the activin and inhibin subunits provide TGF-beta family signals that suppress lymphoid differentiation, SFRP1 dampens Wnt signalling in the marrow niche, and HMGB3 keeps progenitors in a less committed state. Complement receptor CR1 links the pathway to immune complex feedback on B cells.

Macrophages amplify inflammation by secreting cytokines, and this braking arm keeps that output proportionate, limiting collateral tissue damage and allowing resolution once a threat is cleared. Loss of such restraint underlies septic shock, chronic inflammatory disease and fibrosis, while excessive restraint leaves macrophages tolerant and poorly responsive to infection. The negative regulation of macrophage cytokine production operates at two levels represented here: an intracellular checkpoint on Toll-like receptor signalling, where IRAK3 acts as a catalytically inactive decoy kinase that blocks downstream NF-κB activation, and CUEDC2 dampens inflammatory transcriptional responses; and secreted control, where the three TGF-beta ligands act on macrophages in an autocrine and paracrine fashion to suppress pro-inflammatory gene expression and push cells toward a reparative, immunosuppressive state. Together these mechanisms set the threshold and duration of innate immune activation.

Interferon-gamma drives macrophage activation, antigen presentation and Th1 immunity, and this braking arm keeps that response proportionate so that inflammation resolves rather than damaging tissue. Damping the cellular reaction to type II interferon limits classical macrophage polarisation and helps preserve an alternative, tissue-repair phenotype; when the brake fails, chronic IFN-gamma signalling contributes to autoimmunity and inflammatory pathology, while excessive braking favours tumour immune evasion and poor control of intracellular pathogens. The mechanisms are varied: a phosphatase dephosphorylates JAK kinases and STAT1 to terminate receptor signalling, nuclear receptors including the two liver X receptors and the adipogenic and anti-inflammatory PPARG transcriptionally oppose interferon-induced gene programmes, an ADP-ribosyltransferase of the macrodomain family biases signalling toward Th2/STAT6 output, and arginase 1 consumes arginine that inducible nitric oxide synthase would otherwise use for antimicrobial killing.

The NLRP3 inflammasome converts danger signals into caspase-1 activation, IL-1β and IL-18 release, and pyroptotic death, so cells need brakes on its assembly to avoid self-damaging inflammation. Restraining that assembly is what keeps sterile injury, crystal deposition and infection from tipping into chronic inflammatory disease; loss of these brakes underlies periodic fever syndromes and contributes to gout, atherosclerosis and neuroinflammation. The restraint works at several levels: ubiquitin ligases such as TRIM31 and FBXL2 target NLRP3 for degradation, autophagy machinery including IRGM and LAMP2-dependent chaperone-mediated autophagy clears the sensor, pyrin-domain-only proteins PYDC1 and PYDC2 act as decoys that block adaptor recruitment, and depalmitoylases together with kinases and SIRT2 tune NLRP3 through reversible lipid and post-translational modification. Other NLR and pyrin-domain proteins, and the microglial receptor TREM2, provide additional inhibitory input, setting the threshold for innate immune activation.

Regulatory T cells restrain immune responses, so the pathways that hold back their differentiation set how much suppression a response is allowed to accumulate. Damping Treg output favours effector T cell expansion and is needed for effective responses to pathogens and tumours, while excessive suppression of Treg development tips the balance toward autoimmunity and tissue damage. Several routes converge here: the OX40 ligand encoded by TNFSF4 signals to conventional T cells and opposes the induced Treg programme, checkpoint receptors such as CTLA4 and LAG3 and the transcription factor IRF1 shape the cytokine and costimulatory environment in which FOXP3 is or is not induced, the growth factor midkine skews differentiation away from the regulatory fate, and microRNAs including miR-21 tune the same decision. Proteasome subunits, including the immunoproteasome catalytic subunits, contribute by degrading lineage-determining factors and controlling antigen presentation.

T cells only reach the right tissue if their motility is switched off at the right moment, and this is the braking side of that decision — processes that reduce the rate or extent of T cell migration. Restraining movement matters for retaining activated cells in lymph nodes, limiting infiltration of inflamed or immunoprivileged tissue, and preventing autoimmune damage; the same brakes, exploited by tumours, keep effector cells out of the tumour bed. CD69 is an early activation marker whose surface expression blocks egress from lymphoid tissue, while CD200 engaging its receptor CD200R1 delivers an inhibitory signal from tissue cells to myeloid and lymphoid cells. RIPOR2 and LRCH1 act inside the cell on Rho-family GTPase signalling to dampen chemokine-driven adhesion and polarisation, linking receptor input to cytoskeletal output.

Th1 responses drive interferon-gamma-dependent defence against intracellular pathogens, but unchecked they cause tissue damage and autoimmunity, so they must be actively restrained; this pathway covers the brakes applied to T-helper 1 type immunity. Several mechanisms appear together. IL-27, formed from EBI3 with its partner chain and signalling through IL27RA with the shared IL6ST subunit, limits Th1 and Th17 differentiation and promotes regulatory programmes. The checkpoint receptor HAVCR2 (TIM-3) engaged by galectin-9 (LGALS9) triggers exhaustion or death of interferon-gamma-producing effector T cells. A soluble binding protein sequesters IL-18, neutralising a cytokine that would otherwise amplify interferon-gamma output, while IL-33 acting through IL1RL1 skews responses toward type 2 immunity. Loss of such restraint underlies chronic inflammatory disease, whereas its excess in tumours blunts protective antitumour T cell activity.

Type I interferon signalling must be shut off once a viral threat is cleared, and this braking programme is what limits it. Sustained interferon output damages tissue and drives autoinflammatory disease: loss of the cytosolic exonuclease TREX1 or the dNTP triphosphohydrolase SAMHD1 leaves self nucleic acids to trigger chronic interferon production, as in Aicardi-Goutières syndrome, while ADAR-mediated RNA editing marks endogenous double-stranded RNA as self so it is not read as viral. Downstream, USP18 removes ISG15 conjugates and independently blocks JAK-STAT engagement at the receptor, and the phosphatase PTPN2 dephosphorylates JAK-STAT components. Additional restraint comes from m6A-dependent decay of interferon transcripts through METTL3 and the YTHDF readers, deadenylation by CNOT7, and translational repression via the EIF4E2-GIGYF2 module. Together these set the amplitude and duration of antiviral gene expression and preserve tolerance to self nucleic acids.

Dendritic cells are the antigen-presenting cells that prime naive T cells, and restraining their differentiation from myeloid progenitors sets how much of that priming capacity a tissue has. Holding this brake in place favours tolerance: fewer, less mature dendritic cells mean weaker T cell activation against self and against transplanted or fetal tissue, while loss of restraint contributes to autoimmunity and unwanted inflammation. The genes involved act at several levels. Inhibitory surface receptors bearing ITIM motifs, including the IgG receptor FCGR2B, the C-type lectin CLEC12A and the leukocyte immunoglobulin-like receptor LILRB1, recruit phosphatases that dampen activating signals; HLA-G is a non-classical MHC class I ligand for such receptors and a mediator of immune privilege. The related membrane proteins TMEM176A and TMEM176B act intracellularly to hold cells in an immature state, and ZBTB46 is a transcription factor marking the classical dendritic cell lineage while limiting its activation.

Monocytes and myeloid progenitors do not become macrophages by default; this is the restraining side of that decision, holding back macrophage differentiation so that progenitors remain available or commit to other fates. Its output matters for the balance of myeloid populations in tissue: too little restraint and inflammatory macrophage numbers expand, which contributes to atherosclerotic plaque growth and adipose tissue inflammation. The mechanisms represented are heterogeneous. Transcriptional control comes from GATA2, which sustains earlier progenitor programmes, and from ZBTB46, which marks and enforces the conventional dendritic cell alternative rather than the macrophage one. Secreted inhibin and activin subunits act on progenitors from outside, and adipocyte-derived adiponectin dampens macrophage development and activation. Post-transcriptional and signalling brakes include the RNA-binding protein QKI and the phosphatase PTPN2, which limits cytokine receptor signalling driving myeloid maturation.

Monocytes are recruited out of the bloodstream toward chemokine gradients at sites of injury and infection, and this recruitment has to be damped as well as driven; damping it is what negative regulation of monocyte chemotaxis does. Restraining monocyte influx limits the tissue damage of prolonged inflammation and shapes how atherosclerotic lesions, fibrotic scars and healing wounds develop, since each depends on how many monocyte-derived macrophages arrive. The activities represented here work at different levels: secreted matricellular and BMP-antagonist proteins such as CCN3, NBL1 and GREM1 act in the extracellular milieu, the repulsive guidance cue SLIT2 signals through Robo receptors to block directed migration of myeloid cells, DUSP1 dephosphorylates MAP kinases to cut short inflammatory signalling, and the immune receptor SLAMF8 tempers macrophage responses. Together they set a brake on innate immune cell trafficking rather than on chemokine production alone.
